planting.note: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before the last frost; this late-maincrop variety needs a long cool season to size up its oblong russet-skinned tubers.

directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in deep, loose, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing rows generously since this vigorous variety produces a heavy underground spread. Maris Piper was bred in Britain in the 1960s and became the standard chip-shop and baking potato across the UK, prized for its high dry-matter content, floury texture, and thin cream-colored skin that crisps well when fried. Hill soil around the stems as they emerge to prevent tuber greening, and expect a longer season than early varieties before the vines die back and tubers can be lifted for storage. Choose this cultivar over a general baking potato when a reliably fluffy, low-moisture interior for chips, roasting, and baking is the priority.

planting.note: Plant certified seed pieces after soil has warmed slightly; as a late maincrop fingerling it needs the longest season of any common salad potato.

directions: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in light, well-drained soil, and be patient, since this is a true late-season variety and tubers will not fully knobble and size up until the last weeks of the growing season. Pink Fir Apple is a Victorian-era heirloom fingerling named for its long, narrow, knobbly tubers with pink-blushed skin and waxy, nutty, pale-yellow flesh that holds its shape beautifully when boiled whole. It remains a favorite of chefs and home cooks for cold potato salads because the dense waxy texture does not turn mealy or fall apart. Choose it over a modern fingerling hybrid when a genuinely old salad-potato flavor and the classic irregular fingerling shape are the goal.

planting.note: Plant certified seed pieces once soil is workable; this vigorous maincrop variety tolerates a wide range of soils better than many modern cultivars.

directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil and hill generously, as this old Scottish cultivar produces a heavy crop of round to oval tubers with distinctive rose-pink skin and creamy white, floury flesh. Bred in Scotland in 1917, Kerr's Pink became a staple maincrop potato across Ireland and Scotland thanks to its reliable yields, good disease tolerance, and adaptability to poorer, wetter soils than many refined modern varieties tolerate. The floury texture makes excellent mash and roast potatoes but causes it to break apart in soups and stews, so reserve it for dry-cooking preparations. Grow it where a rustic, high-yielding heirloom maincrop with real cold-region pedigree is wanted over a fussier modern hybrid.

planting.note: Plant certified seed pieces once soil is workable; this maincrop heirloom needs a full cool season to develop its solid red interior color.

directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; this British heirloom is one of the few potato cultivars with deep burgundy-red flesh that runs solidly through the tuber rather than just tinting the skin. The color, driven by anthocyanin pigments, fades only slightly with cooking, producing striking pink-tinged mash, roasted wedges, and chips. Flavor is earthy and slightly nutty with a moderately dry, floury texture suited to baking and roasting more than boiling. Grow it as a novelty maincrop alongside white- and yellow-fleshed varieties for a dramatic color contrast at harvest and on the plate.

planting.note: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before the last frost; this mid-season heirloom performs well in cooler northern climates as well as short winter-growing regions.

directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Yellow Finn is a Finnish heirloom predating the modern yellow-flesh varieties it helped inspire, producing round to oval tubers with tan skin and dense, buttery-yellow flesh. The flavor is rich and naturally buttery even without added fat, and the moderately waxy texture holds together well for potato salad while still mashing smoothly. It stores well for a fingerling-adjacent heirloom and tends to be more drought-tolerant than many modern hybrids once established. Choose it over Yukon Gold when a true heirloom lineage and slightly denser, more old-fashioned texture are preferred.

planting.note: Plant certified seed pieces once soil is workable; this early-to-mid season red potato sizes up quickly for a June or early-summer harvest.

directions: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; Sangre is a Colorado-bred round red potato developed for the western US fresh-market trade, prized for its smooth, bright red skin and shallow eyes that make for clean, attractive market tubers. The white flesh is moderately moist and holds its shape well when boiled, making it a solid choice for potato salads, roasting, and general table use. It bulks up earlier than many maincrop reds, making it a good option where an early harvest of good-looking red new potatoes is wanted. Grow it alongside a russet or yellow variety for a mixed-color early harvest.

planting.note: Plant certified seed pieces after the soil has warmed slightly; this late fingerling needs a long full season to fill out its knobby tubers.

directions: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; Ozette is descended from fingerling potatoes brought to the Pacific Northwest coast by Spanish explorers in the late 1700s and preserved for generations by the Makah Tribe near Neah Bay, Washington. The tubers are long, narrow, and knobby with tan skin and dense, waxy, slightly nutty yellow flesh that holds together well when steamed or roasted whole. It is listed on the Slow Food USA Ark of Taste as a culturally significant heirloom variety worth preserving in home gardens. Grow it for its genuine Indigenous heritage and distinctive narrow fingerling shape rather than for high yield, since production is modest compared to modern cultivars.
sources: Slow Food USA - Ark of Taste

planting.note: Plant certified seed pieces once soil is workable; this mid-season red round variety is well suited to northern-tier growing regions.

directions: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; Chieftain is a red-skinned, white-fleshed round potato released from a USDA and North Dakota State University breeding program in the 1960s for the Upper Midwest fresh market. The smooth, deep red skin holds its color well in storage, and the moist, moderately waxy flesh boils cleanly without excessive breakdown, making it a dependable variety for potato salad and general table use. It has a strong reputation among northern growers for consistent yields and good storage quality compared to older red cultivars of its era. Choose it over Red Norland or Red Pontiac when a slightly later, higher-yielding red round is wanted for storage rather than earliest harvest.
